checkpoints: The root problem isn't any particular service — it's that the design is missing a single entry point.

First problem, topology coupling: the client knows the host/port of every service ahead of time, so every time a service is added, an address changes, or a security rule is added, every client already deployed out there has to be updated — the bigger the system, the more places have to change.
Second problem, duplicated shared logic: auth, rate limiting, CORS, TLS termination, logging get copied into every service, and those copies gradually drift apart when nobody syncs them by hand.

An API gateway fixes the topology problem by standing between the client and the service cluster: the client now knows only one address, all internal hosts/ports/service count stay hidden, and adding a new service is just one route entry — the client changes nothing.
It fixes the duplication problem too: the shared concerns get written exactly once at the edge and then apply to every service behind it, instead of being repeated N times.
The responsibility boundary is clean: the gateway only transports and protects (routing + cross-cutting concerns) while business logic still belongs to the service.
The gateway behaves as a transparent reverse proxy, relaying method, body, and status code verbatim, never interpreting or altering the result.

In exchange, the gateway becomes a point that can bring down the whole system (a potential SPOF) and adds one latency hop to every request — mitigated in practice by running multiple gateway replicas behind a load balancer with health checks for failover.
Synchronous request/response is tightly coupled in time — the caller must wait for the receiver.
A slow or dead downstream hangs the whole flow, even though that downstream (e.g. sending a notification) has nothing to do with whether the order itself is valid.
Asynchronous event-driven inverts that temporal dependency: the producer just appends a fact that already happened (e.g. "ORDER_CREATED") to a durable topic and returns immediately.
Consumers process the event later at their own pace and need not be online at the exact moment it is published.
The price is that the client sees PENDING rather than "fully processed" — the system becomes eventually consistent.
This trades instantaneity for fault tolerance and availability.
A concrete payoff of the durable log: a consumer offline at publish time replays from its committed offset once it comes back, losing nothing.

Message brokers like Kafka guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once — a consumer restart, a rebalance, or a retry after an ack timeout can redeliver the same event, so any handler that performs a side effect without a duplicate check will re-execute that side effect on every redelivery.

Both handlers here execute unconditionally: the `ORDER_CREATED` branch never checks for an existing payment row before `create`-ing one, so a redelivered event produces a second row and captures the card twice; the `INVENTORY_OUT_OF_STOCK` branch never checks whether the row is already `REFUNDED` before setting it to `REFUNDED` again, so a redelivered event re-emits `PAYMENT_REFUNDED` and can trigger a duplicate refund.

Making a handler idempotent means deduping by a stable business or correlation id — such as `orderId` or `eventId` — and guarding the state transition so the operation is skipped when the current status already shows it happened, turning a repeated event into a safe no-op instead of a duplicate side effect.

A compensating transaction (the refund) is a brand-new, independent local transaction that inverts the effect of the original capture across a different piece of state — it is not a distributed `ROLLBACK` — so it needs its own idempotency guard rather than inheriting safety from being labeled the undo step.

Because a broker can reorder events across partitions, a compensation event like `INVENTORY_OUT_OF_STOCK` can arrive before the corresponding `ORDER_CREATED` capture has been persisted; calling `findOne` in that case returns nothing, and immediately mutating the missing row throws and crashes the consumer mid-saga.

When compensation runs before its target row exists, the correct behavior is to treat that as a valid, retryable state and return cleanly without throwing, so the event can be reprocessed once the capture eventually commits rather than crashing the service.

Producers should key saga events by `orderId` so every event belonging to the same saga lands on the same partition, preserving the relative order between a capture and the compensating refund meant to undo it.

Idempotency can be verified by redelivering the same event twice and asserting exactly one capture or refund occurred, by replaying events out of order and asserting no crash or orphaned/double compensation results, and by routing a compensation that keeps failing to a dead-letter topic instead of silently dropping it.

Replaying an event-sourced aggregate by folding every event from version 1 on each read makes the read cost O(n) in the total number of events ever written, not in the size of the answer actually needed — so latency grows purely because the append-only log keeps getting longer.

Because an event log is append-only, the event count n never shrinks, so a replay-from-scratch load path has no ceiling: an account that has accumulated thousands of events pays for its entire history on every single read, even when only the current balance is needed.

A snapshot is a periodically persisted copy of the aggregate's state at a given version (for example every 10 events) written to a separate store; the load path then starts from the latest snapshot's state and folds only the events after that version, bounding replay work to the tail of the log instead of the whole history.

A snapshot must remain a derived cache, never the source of truth: the event log stays append-only and untouched, and deleting every snapshot must still let the system rebuild identical state by replaying from the log — if the state differs without snapshots, the snapshot has silently become authoritative.

Snapshotting introduces trade-offs: extra storage for the snapshot table, a background job that must reliably fire after each qualifying write, and a staleness window bounded by the snapshot interval (at most the events between the last snapshot and the current version), which the tail replay always closes.

Correctness of a snapshot mechanism is verified by wiping the snapshot store, forcing the load path back onto full replay, and asserting the resulting state exactly matches the snapshot-backed path — this is the test that proves the snapshot never replaced the event log as ground truth.

The performance benefit of snapshotting is verified by benchmarking load latency on a high-version account before and after enabling snapshots: the latency curve should flatten to roughly constant cost instead of continuing to grow linearly with the number of events.

Fixing this kind of unbounded-replay cost starts with measuring where the cost actually comes from — confirming that the fold over the full event array, not network or serialization overhead, is what scales with n — before introducing snapshotting as the remedy.

The rebuild's slowdown comes from three costs compounding together, not from a single bottleneck: a forced flush on every single write, one network round-trip per document instead of batching, and writing directly into the live index that ordinary queries are still hitting.

Passing `refresh: true` on every `esClient.index()` call forces Elasticsearch to flush a new searchable segment after each individual document — an operation expensive enough that it is meant to be paid once per batch, not once per row, so over a real-sized history it adds up to thousands of unnecessary flushes.
Indexing documents one at a time instead of through the bulk API wastes a full network round-trip per row, multiplying overhead across the entire history being replayed.

The fix for the write-side cost is to switch to the bulk API (`esClient.helpers.bulk` or `esClient.bulk`) to batch hundreds of documents per request, drop `refresh: true`, and optionally set `refresh_interval: -1` on the target index during the load, refreshing once at the end — this removes almost all the flush and round-trip overhead.

Rebuilding into the same `'customers'` index that `GET /customer/:id` reads from makes every in-flight query compete with the rebuild for that index's resources, and a query landing mid-rebuild sees whatever partial subset has been re-indexed so far — a half-populated read model exposed to live traffic.

A zero-downtime reindex builds a brand-new index (e.g. `customers_v2`) off to the side, bulk-loads the entire history into it, and then atomically repoints the `customers` alias from the old index to the new one via a single `indices.updateAliases` call, so the swap is instantaneous and clients never observe a partial index.

This full rebuild is safe specifically because of CQRS: the read model in Elasticsearch is a derived, idempotent, upsert-by-id projection of the write model in Postgres, so the write model itself is never touched and a from-scratch reindex risks nothing on the source of truth.

Verifying the fix means confirming query latency stays flat throughout the bulk-and-swap rebuild, that the alias flip happens as a single atomic call with no window where `customers` resolves to nothing, and that the new index's document count matches `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers` before the alias is flipped.
Build ONE aggregation endpoint (e.g. GET /order-detail?orderId=) that the mobile client calls once, instead of three sequential round-trips to order/product/user services over a weak connection.
Internally the endpoint fans out to the three services in PARALLEL, each branch carrying its own timeout, so overall latency is bounded by the slowest branch rather than the sum of all three.
Add a circuit breaker per branch so one dead/slow service fails fast instead of hanging the whole endpoint.

On partial failure (e.g. product service times out), don't return a 500 for the whole response — return what succeeded (order + user) and flag the failed section so the client can show a placeholder/skeleton for just that part.
Merge the results into one payload shaped specifically for the order-detail screen.

Put this aggregation in a dedicated mobile BFF rather than the shared API gateway: merging forces knowledge of three services' shapes; stuffing that into the shared gateway would force it to know every client's shape and keep growing, whereas a per-client BFF keeps the merge thin at the cost of one more artifact — an acceptable trade.

The BFF must never absorb business logic — it only composes/trims data at the transport layer; a rule like "order always starts PENDING" belongs to the order service, not the BFF, or the BFF becomes a disguised monolith hard to test/scale.

The event envelope has: aggregate_id (groups events per aggregate), monotonic version (orders events within the aggregate), event_type (names the fact), payload e.g. JSONB (business data), occurred_at (system-assigned timestamp), and eventVersion (for future schema evolution).
None of these fields is ever UPDATEd or DELETEd, because the whole point of event sourcing is a log that only grows, never corrected in place.

Command → event boundary: a command expresses INTENT and is validated against state replayed fresh from the log — it can be rejected (e.g. withdrawing beyond the balance errors out and no event is written).

Only once validation passes does the handler append exactly one event — a FACT that happened — and once appended that event is permanent; business logic/validation live on the command side, so there is no such thing as a "failed withdrawal" event in the log.

Concurrency: enforce a UNIQUE (aggregate_id, version) constraint as the final safety net, plus serialize writers per aggregate (e.g. reading MAX(version) under a per-aggregate lock like pg_advisory_xact_lock) before writing the next version.
This is optimistic concurrency: if two writes collide on a version, the losing request errors and must retry, so two events never share the same version.

Schema evolution: never edit a written event (destroys immutability/audit trail); when an event's shape must change, add eventVersion to the payload plus an upcaster layer that translates old-shaped events to the new shape at replay time, keeping applyEvent backward-compatible with missing fields on older events.

The whole contract only holds if the log is the single source of truth and state/read-models are derived projections (a fold/reduce over the log); the append path must be the system's only write door, and every projection must always be rebuildable from scratch without migrating the underlying data.
The publisher (signup) only emits the event onto a logical subject — it never calls anyone by name and never knows how many subscribers are listening.
Adding fraud-detection is purely a matter of standing up a new service that registers its own listener on the same subject — the signup code stays untouched.

Pub/sub replaces address coupling (knowing exactly who to call) with contract coupling (agreeing on subject name and message shape), so the set of consumers can grow independently without dragging the publisher along.
Contrast: if signup called downstreams directly, every new consumer would force a rewrite of the signup code.
And with direct calls, the whole signup request would be dragged along by whichever downstream happens to be slowest — exactly the coupling pub/sub eliminates.
At its core, a single emit is broadcast to every subscriber currently online on that subject (1 message → N receivers), unlike a queue, where each message is delivered to exactly one consumer.

Returning HTTP 200 with an empty object when the id doesn't exist is a bug: the client reads 200 as "success" and can no longer tell "found but empty" apart from "does not exist", so downstream logic silently misbehaves with no exception ever thrown.
The Gateway's real job at the edge is status translation: map the id:0 sentinel or gRPC NOT_FOUND to HTTP 404, INVALID_ARGUMENT to 400, and so on.
The HTTP status code is the contract with the client, while the gRPC status is purely an internal concern between the Gateway and the backend that must never leak through unchanged.
REST/JSON is universal, browsers call it natively, and it's easy to debug and cache — so it belongs at the edge facing the client.

gRPC runs HTTP/2 + binary Protobuf, fast and strongly typed — so it belongs at the core, service-to-service; the Gateway is the handoff point translating both protocol and status between the two worlds.
A REST Gateway exists at all because the browser can't speak gRPC directly — it can't control the HTTP/2 frames/trailers gRPC needs, so it would require gRPC-Web plus a translating proxy.
Reject the shortcut: Database-per-Service means each service's database is private — no other service may access it directly.
This isolation lets a service change its internal schema (or even swap its database engine) without any other service breaking.
Because the data lives in separate databases, a single SQL JOIN spanning two services becomes technically impossible.
This impossibility is framed as an intentional feature forcing explicit contracts, not a limitation to quietly work around.
API composition is one legitimate way to combine data: query each service's own API separately and merge results in the application layer.
CQRS read model is the other legitimate way: a service subscribes to the other services' events and pre-materializes its own joined read view ahead of time.
Because sync happens via events after the fact, the combined result reflects eventual consistency, not instant correctness.

The net trade-off: giving up centralized transactions and JOIN convenience buys per-service independence (own database tech, own deploy/scale, isolated failures) at the cost of owning consistency yourself.
